title: Or — devotion to Ishvara (1.23–1.26)
hook: after all the talk of effort and intensity, Patanjali adds one small word, or, and opens a second road
tomorrow: Om is his name; repeat it; know its meaning

segments.voice: Yesterday: the born-free and the rest of us, shraddha, faith, energy, memory, gathering, wisdom, and the dial of mild, medium, intense. Did you turn one effort up a notch? Today, a different road. Day four hundred thirty-six.
screen: `THE BORN-FREE AND THE REST OF US.`

segments.voice: Sutra after sutra, Patanjali has been talking like a coach. Practice long, without breaks. Let go of thirst. Bring faith, energy, memory. Turn up the intensity. It's a lot of effort, and you might start to feel the weight of it. And then, in sutra 1.23, a tiny Sanskrit word, va. It means or. One syllable in either language, and it changes the whole tone. Or, the sutra says, there is another way.
screen: `PRACTICE. LET GO. TURN IT UP.` → `THEN ONE SMALL WORD.` → `VA: OR.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.23: ishvara pranidhanad va. Or, by devotion to Ishvara. Ishvara means the Lord. Pranidhana means placing yourself before, setting yourself down in front of, so devotion, surrender, dedication. The commentator Vyasa explains why this is a shortcut. Through this special devotion, he says, the Lord turns toward the practitioner and favors them, by his will alone, and absorption becomes near. So this road is not only your effort. It's met from the other side. Then Patanjali tells you who Ishvara is, in three short sutras. 1.24: a special kind of purusha, a special seer, untouched by afflictions, by actions, by their fruits and by the traces they leave. 1.25: in Ishvara, the seed of all-knowing is unsurpassed. 1.26: the teacher even of the most ancient teachers, because Ishvara is not limited by time. Notice what's not said. Ishvara here is not described as the creator of the world, and Patanjali doesn't name a particular god. Scholars debate how central Ishvara is to the whole text: some read the yoga of Patanjali as deeply theistic, others as a method in which devotion is one powerful option among several. Hindu teachers in many lineages take it as a real invitation to bhakti, the word you met at the end of the Shvetashvatara. Either way, the sutra leaves a tired practitioner a second road, one that doesn't rest on effort alone. Or.
screen: `VA: OR. A SECOND ROAD.` · `PRANIDHANA: SETTING YOURSELF DOWN BEFORE.` · `UNTOUCHED, ALL-KNOWING, THE FIRST TEACHER.` · then, large: `MET FROM THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. For the first part of this sit, try hard: keep returning to the breath, alert, effortful. Then, halfway through, change the posture inside. Imagine setting yourself down in front of something greater than you, the way you'd set down a heavy bag. If you pray, place yourself before God as you know God. If not, place yourself before the stillness itself. Let the effort soften. Notice what changes. The bell holds the time.
Or. The small word va in sutra 1.23 that opens a second road: devotion to Ishvara, the Lord, who meets the practitioner from the other side.

Your line: the shortcut. Today, when something feels like it all depends on you, try the second road for one minute: set it down for a moment, before God if you pray, or simply in a pause, and see what's still yours to do. Day four hundred thirty-six.

screen: `DAY 436 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: OM IS HIS NAME; REPEAT IT; KNOW ITS MEANING.`

howItsDone: Many Hindu yoga lineages treat ishvara pranidhana as central, practiced through prayer, offering one's actions to God, and repeating a divine name, while others teach it as one of several supports for meditation.

pairs: teacher of the ancients, beyond time

myth: Patanjali describes Ishvara as the creator of the world
the sutras describe a special purusha, all-knowing and the first teacher, but not as creator.
Vyasa says the Lord favors the devoted practitioner
the Lord turns toward them and absorption becomes near.
pranidhana means setting yourself down before, devotion
placing yourself in front of the Lord: surrender, dedication.

fork.setup: you've practiced with all your effort, and you're worn out. sutra 1.23 offers something else. what?
options: devotion to Ishvara: a road met from the other side.
fork.reveal: or, by devotion to Ishvara. Vyasa says the Lord turns toward the devoted one, and absorption comes near.

original.note: Sanskrit īśvara: the Lord, the one who is able. in the Yoga Sutras, a special purusha, the first teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'or' is just a connecting word.
what it means: a second road, devotion, beside effort and intensity.
what a scholar hears: Ishvara is defined as a purusha-vishesha, 'a special seer', not as creator; how theistic Patanjali's system is remains debated, and Vyasa reads 1.23 as grace (anugraha).

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.23–1.26 (devotion to Ishvara; who Ishvara is)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.23 (the Lord favors the devoted one)

notes: Editor review (y2 pass): cut the narrator's 'every tired practitioner learns: you don't have to do it all alone' (an 'every' claim that pushed belief); the carry now offers the second road with or without prayer.
Debate over the role of Ishvara (theistic vs. one option among methods) is stated without ranking.
Ishvara as 'not creator' in Patanjali: standard reading; some later commentators (e.g. Vijnanabhikshu) give Ishvara a larger cosmic role. Please check.
